sources.title: National Register of Historic Places listings in Clark County, Nevada
Category:Buildings and structures in Las Vegas

stops.name: Golden Gate Hotel and Casino
stops.description: The oldest hotel and casino in Las Vegas, open on this corner since 1906 and the place that put the fifty-cent shrimp cocktail on the map.

stops.name: Fremont Street Experience
stops.description: Five blocks of old Fremont Street were closed to cars and roofed with a barrel canopy 1,375 feet long that now carries roughly 49 million LEDs.

stops.name: Vegas Vic
stops.description: The waving neon cowboy has stood over this corner since 1951 and was relit in 2023 after a spell dark.

stops.name: Binion's Gambling Hall and Hotel
stops.description: Benny Binion opened here in 1951, was the first downtown house to carpet over its sawdust floors, and ran the World Series of Poker from these tables for 35 years.

stops.name: Golden Nugget Las Vegas
stops.description: Open since 1946, its lobby holds the Hand of Faith, an 875-troy-ounce lump of Australian gold billed as the largest nugget on public display anywhere.

stops.name: Mob Museum
stops.description: The 1933 federal post office and courthouse, where one of the Kefauver organized crime hearings was gavelled in, has told the story of the mob from inside its own courtroom since 2012.

stops.name: El Cortez Hotel and Casino
stops.description: Downtown's first full resort, open since 1941 and briefly owned by Bugsy Siegel and Meyer Lansky, wearing a facade almost nobody in this town has left alone as long.

stops.name: Downtown Container Park
stops.description: Shops and bars stacked out of 43 shipping containers, guarded at the gate by a Burning Man praying mantis that shoots fire from its antennae.

stops.name: Atomic Liquors
stops.description: The oldest freestanding bar in Las Vegas, licensed in 1952 and named for the drinkers who climbed onto its roof to watch the test-site mushroom clouds.

stops.name: Old Las Vegas Mormon Fort State Historic Park
stops.description: A surviving adobe building from the 1855 Mormon mission, the oldest structure in the valley and the reason there is a city here at all.

stops.name: The Neon Museum
stops.description: More than 200 rescued signs from dead casinos and motels lie in an outdoor boneyard, greeted by the salvaged shell-shaped lobby of the La Concha Motel.

stops.name: The Smith Center for the Performing Arts
stops.description: An art deco hall opened in 2012 whose 17-story tower carries 47 bells across four octaves, rung over a neighbourhood built on old railyard land.

stops.name: Cleveland Clinic Lou Ruvo Center for Brain Health
stops.description: Frank Gehry split this 2010 building in two, a plain clinic beside a crumpled steel shell, a deliberate nod to the two halves of the brain treated inside.

stops.name: Las Vegas High School Academic Building
stops.description: The town's first high school, opened in 1931 and now the Las Vegas Academy of the Arts, is the best art deco building left in the city.

stops.name: Morelli House
stops.description: The 1959 mid-century home of Sands bandleader Antonio Morelli, where the Rat Pack drank after the late show, moved here brick by brick from the Desert Inn golf course in 2001.

note: Las Vegas is the alphabetically first NFL host city that has never had a run; the sweep worked alphabetically through Kansas City yesterday. All 15 stops sit inside a rough one-mile square of downtown, bounded by Symphony Park on the west, 9th Street on the east, Washington Avenue on the north and Bridger Avenue on the south, so the north pair (Old Mormon Fort, Neon Museum) adds about half a mile to a walk that otherwise stays on the Fremont Street corridor. Every stop has a street address and a ZIP. Deliberately excluded: the whole Strip, because Mandalay Bay, Allegiant Stadium, the Bellagio fountains and the rest sit in Paradise or Winchester rather than the city of Las Vegas, and filing them under Las Vegas would be wrong on the city field. Also dropped as outliers more than a mile out: Huntridge Theater (1208 E Charleston Blvd), the Green Shack (2504 E Fremont St), Moulin Rouge Hotel (900 W Bonanza Rd, and the building burned in 2003 and 2009 with little left to stand in front of), Woodlawn Cemetery and Berkley Square. The Punk Rock Museum and the 18b Arts District are a genuine second cluster about three quarters of a mile south of Fremont and are worth a run of their own if a second Las Vegas path is ever wanted.
